articles.title: Democrats take control of US Congress in major rebuke of Trump. What comes next?
articles.author: Devin B. Martinez
articles.content: Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the country’s midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, in a crushing rebuke of US President Donald Trump’s second term. The Republicans lost at least seven Senate seats in states that have traditionally been strongholds for the right-wing party. The party also lost over two dozen House districts to the Democrats. In the 2024 presidential election, Trump had won some of these districts by double-digit percentage points. Kansas will have a Democratic senator for the first time in nearly a century. North and South Carolina and even Texas have flipped to the Democrats in an unprecedented shift for those states. The sweeping defeat comes after $12 billion dollars was spent. mostly by billionaires on both sides of the aisle, on what analysts are calling the most expensive midterm elections in history. A condemnation of Trump and the administration’s priorities A total of 435 seats in the US House of Representatives were up for election and 35 seats of the US Senate’s 100 seats were also decided. These two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives, make up the US Congress. While the president himself is not up for election, various analysts have characterized these midterm elections as a referendum on US President Donald Trump. And the resounding defeat for the Republican Party is seen as a profound rejection of the administration and its priorities over the last two years. Corruption, inflation, rising fuel prices, and the Iran war are cited as some of the top concerns on voters’ minds. “The reason we lost is the war,” said Vice President JD Vance in a post online. Speaking to BreakThrough News on election night, Trita Parsi, Iranian-Swedish international relations writer and political analyst, spoke about the deep unpopularity of the Iran war as a driver of the election result. “I don’t think we have seen an election in recent memory in which the war is such a decisive issue – not a factor – but a decisive issue.” Parsi also spoke about President Trump’s claim just before elections on a morning talk show that US funding to Israel will cease by the end of 2026. This funding is another widely unpopular aspect of US policy. “The Israelis came to the conclusion over a year ago that they have lost the American public,” he said. The plan is to “hide the money,” using joint ventures inside the Pentagon budget in a way that is “outside of the scrutiny of Congress” and the American public. He argued that funding could actually increase through this model. Because support for Israel has become such a political liability, Amanda Yee, host of The China Report , explained that AIPAC announced in October that it would stop making endorsements and direct donations to candidates. “AIPAC isn’t actually stopping any of its spending, it’s just changing the way that it spends,” Yee said. She said the United Democracy Project (UDP), AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC, now operates as a “cover for AIPAC money.” UDP has already spent millions to unseat representatives critical of Israel, such as Jamaal Bowman and Cori Bush. Israel and foreign policy aren’t the only points of dissatisfaction for people in the US, however. Various domestic issues have become major political pressure points US politics, one of the biggest ones is related to AI development. AI data centers become a national flashpoint John Russell, a journalist with More Perfect Union , spoke to BreakThrough News about the increasingly unpopular development of hyper-scale data centers to power the AI boom. He said data centers are “job-killing super computers” that “explode your utility rates” if they are hooked up to the grid next to you. If they’re not hooked up to the grid, then the massive power plants they require “burn dirty fossil fuels that kill our planet.” All of these impacts sustain vast computing that is “just shoveling money up to the top of the economy, to the already fantastically rich.” “This is a uniting issue no matter who you’re voting for,” Russell said. “People can see that this is just a big club and we’re not in it. Russell argued that despite the Democratic Party claiming victory in these elections, the masses of working people are actually looking for a party that will stop “the absolute gains for the richest people on earth” and do something that actually makes life easier and more affordable for the majority. Democrats attack independent socialist candidates and the left During the BreakThrough News election coverage, Zoe Alexandra highlighted a bizarre “mailer-gate” scandal during a race in the state of Ohio that has drawn condemnation of both the Republican and Democratic parties. The Ohio Senate race, won by Democrat Sherrod Brown, involved not just Republican Jon Husted, but also independent socialist candidate Greg Levy, who received 94,509 votes. https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfTa0tNM0tE/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&obrf=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==&srtk=MzRlODBiNWFlZA== In this “mailer-gate” scandal, a MAGA-linked super PAC spent 2 million dollars on mailers that mimicked Greg Levy’s socialist platform. “Mailers and video ads called on voters to ‘Join the Revolution’ and support socialist candidate Greg Levy” and criticized Sherrod Brown for being anti-worker, Alexandra said. The BT journalist said the maneuver was immediately condemned by Greg Levy and his team, who called it “a dirty trick” and a form of “digital blackface.” However, Alexandra emphasized that the Democrats’ response was not to join Levy and condemn the Republicans’ dirty electoral maneuver. “Instead, the Democrats decided to turn on Greg Levy,” Alexandra said. “They went on the offensive and were very quick to say ‘Gregy Levy is working with Republicans’ and ‘Greg Levy is actually your enemy.’” She demonstrated various mailers that the Democrats paid for to disseminate these messages. Alexandra also demonstrated headlines by corporate media outlets that blame socialist Greg Levy for potentially “spoiling” the Democratic victory in the state. A Newsweek headline read, “How a Socialist Could Undermine Sherrod Brown’s Ohio Comeback.” Another headline in The Washington Post read “PAC linked to GOP firm is boosting Ohio socialist in Senate race.” The Sherrod Brown campaign went as far as taking out an attack video ad, that spread fear and suspicion about the Greg Levy campaign being influenced by the Republican Party to “split the tides” in the Ohio race. “This is where they are directing their money,” Alexandra said. “Instead of the Democrats actually looking at their own race and asking, ‘Why is it that a socialist who’s saying we should have healthcare and education and not go to war is somehow becoming more popular?’ They’re saying, ‘Let’s attack him!’” When it comes to both of the major corporate parties in the US, “they clearly are aligned on one thing which is that the left is a threat to their survival.” Various guests on the show also spoke to the “war on the left” by the Trump administration and the far right and pointed out that if Democrats control both chambers, they would theoretically be able to do something to stand against the political repression of activism and progressivism in the US, although they have shown no opposition to that trend so far. In yet another bold independent socialist campaign in the Bronx (New York’s House District 15) Andre Easton received 8.7% of the vote. He challenged Democratic incumbent Ritchie Torres, who was re-elected, but is increasingly unpopular because of his staunch pro-Israel stance and his consistant attacks on the left and progressive candidates, including Andre Easton. Easton told BreakThrough News that it is the mass movement of workers throughout the other 365 days of the year and the multiple years between elections that truly produces the change people want to see. “Your political responsibility exists beyond the ballot box,” Easton said. He added people should absolutely vote and mobilize their communities to vote. “But your political responsibility is so much more robust and so much wider and deeper than just a single bubble on a sheet.” The socialist Bronx candidate says our political duty is carried out in “our streets, in our communities, in our classrooms and workplaces.” He emphasized that his party, the Party for Socialism and Liberation, is committed to that work and will continue to do so every day after the midterm elections. Renewing their commitment to organizing and mobilizing, various activists, journalists, and progressives have highlighted the limited progress that this crushing victory for Trump represents. What does it actually mean for Democrats to control the US Congress? Now that Democrats have decisively won midterm elections, a key question that has emerged is what can people actually expect from Democratic control of the US Congress? BreakThrough News Editor-and-Chief Ben Becker pointed out that historically, the Democrats’ have failed to use their majorities to advance meaningful progressive change. “It feels good to see Republicans lose, but I don’t think we should translate that feeling into an irrational sense of hope in what the Democrats are going to be able to achieve or even want to achieve.” He highlighted the euphoria for the Democrats winning the House and the Senate after the 2006 midterms, and even more so in the 2008 presidential election. They also had a majority when Joe Biden was elected in 2020. “None of those promises were delivered,” Becker said. “Wether it was student debt relief, universal healthcare, parental leave, universal childcare, climate legislation, immigration reform, codifying roe v wade, we could go down the list.” This gridlock and “failure to deliver,” he argues, created the conditions for Trump to return with a far more extreme right-wing program in the first place. “The euphoria – if it leads to sitting back and hoping the Democrats will do well – it will actually just lead to the return of the Republicans and Trumpism or even something worse than Trumpism.”

articles.title: The ‘blue wave’ is a defeat for Israel, but the left’s work is just beginning
articles.author: Michael Arria
articles.content: Political consultant Peter Feld says the midterms were a rebuke of Trump, the Iran war, and Israel. But with AIPAC adapting and J Street rising, he warns progressives must push for a full arms embargo and resist the capture of their new champions.

articles.title: BT Live: US midterm elections show
articles.author: Zoe.
articles.content: The Democratic Party won big on Tuesday, November 3, winning a majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, and unseating Republicans in historically red states. BreakThrough News hosted a special midterm elections show with Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra bringing you the results as they came in and discussing critical issues shaping the election, including the war on Iran, Palestine, data centers, ICE, healthcare, labor struggles, and so much more. Special Guests included: Jamaal Bowman, former Congressional Representative Trita Parsi, Executive Vice President of the Quincy Institute Katie Halper, Host of The Katie Halper Show John Russell, Emmy-award winning labor journalist and author of The Holler Newsletter Claudia de la Cruz, former presidential candidate Erik Sperling, Executive Director of Just Foreign Policy Andre Easton, Teacher and Congressional candidate challenging Ritichie Torres Amanda Yee, Host of The China Report on BreakThrough News Ben Becker, Editor-in-Chief of BreakThrough News

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed Becomes First Muslim Senator as Democrats Rout GOP Across the U.S. in Rebuke to Trump
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. ANJALI KAMAT : In a stunning rebuke of President Trump and his MAGA movement, Democrats regained control of the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats have picked up at least seven Senate seats, winning Republican seats in Texas, Maine, Ohio, South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa and Kansas. We begin today’s show in Michigan, where progressive Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican former Congressmember Mike Rogers. El-Sayed campaigned on a platform of Medicare for All, ending military aid to Israel, and getting money out of politics. He becomes the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed faced racist, Islamophobic and vitriolic attacks by top Republicans, led by President Trump, who mocked El-Sayed’s name and Muslim faith. During the Democratic primary, AIPAC , the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, spent over $30 million to help El-Sayed’s rival, Haley Stevens. On Sunday, Haley Stevens shocked many by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over El-Sayed. Early this morning, Dr. El-Sayed addressed supporters in Detroit. SEN .- ELECT ABDUL EL- SAYED : My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan. … You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates. So, thank you. This is all yours. Michigan, I cannot wait to serve you with the same big-heartedness, open-mindedness, grit and earnestness that you’ve shown me. … They might have been pointing to my name and my faith, but we all know that my name and my faith aren’t the reason you can’t afford your gas, not the reason you can’t afford your groceries, not the reason you can’t see a doctor. … They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars. If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination, that’s not hate, it’s love. Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here, for schools here and healthcare here and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war. AMY GOODMAN : We go now to Michigan, where we’re joined by Linda Sarsour, who’s been campaigning with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. She is a Palestinian American Muslim organizer, author of We Are Not Here to Be Bystanders , co-founder of MPower Action Fund. Linda, thanks so much for joining us again. We spoke to you last night in the middle of the watch party. It had not been announced yet that the doctor had won. Can you talk about the significance of his victory amidst this enormous onslaught against him, beginning with the president of the United States, who kept calling him Mohamed, saying he could call him that because he’s president of the United States? LINDA SARSOUR : It’s incredible. You could hear it in my voice, Amy. It was a long night, but incredibly worth it. To elect the first Muslim American to the United States Senate is no easy feat in a country that has the most powerful people spewing anti-Muslim hate. We watched this in the last couple of months against Abdul, against his family and against our communities, against organizers, because we are participating in democracy, because we are organizing and building power for things that are going to help our neighbors. We are organizing for our immigrant neighbors, to protect our immigrant neighbors, to abolish ICE , for Medicare for All and to end all military aid to Israel. So, last night wasn’t just about Dr. Abdulrahman being a Muslim, winning and going to the United States Senate, although that in itself is very significant and a rebuke of the bigotry and the racism, and a message to our children that you, too, can grow up and have a name like Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed and go to the United States Senate, and maybe even one day being the president of the United States of America. But more so, it demonstrated that progressives can win in states like Michigan. Michigan is a swing state. And as you remember, Amy, during the 2024 election, people said that Palestine was a losing issue, that Gaza was a losing issue. And now we are demonstrating in this past cycle across the country, from New York City to Colorado to Fresno, California, to Dallas, Texas, that we can win on standing up for the human rights of the Palestinian people. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Linda, you’ve been on the ground campaigning in Michigan with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for his campaign. What were you hearing from voters, I mean, amidst all of this hate? When we spoke a few days ago, you talked about how the mood was quite dark because there were all these negative flyers everywhere. Can you talk about how voters rejected this hate? LINDA SARSOUR : It was outstanding just to see how Dr. Abdul kind of emerged out of this darkness, this kind of cloud of hate, divisiveness, propaganda. If you turned on the television here in Michigan, literally — and I’m not exaggerating — there would be at least 10 ads back to back that were anti-Abdul El-Sayed. It was just horrific, mailers calling him a communist, calling him a radical, doing guilt by association with organizations, political parties around the world, with people. I mean, it was just outrageous on so many levels. And I think what happened here in Michigan is that the voters were sick and tired. It’s not — like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed said, it’s not because his name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed that their gas prices are high or that their electric bills are high or that they’re struggling here. They resonated with this idea that our taxpayer dollars should be going to public schools, should be going to hospitals, and not going to bomb children in Gaza. So, again, the propaganda, the mailers, the digital ads, your algorithms — even when you are not from Michigan, you’re in the state, the algorithm for your digital ads come up as anti-Abdul. But I believed in the voters. I truly believed in them. And they made us all proud, sending Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to the United States Senate. And it’s a message that being anti-Muslim, targeting a minority community in this country, being pro-genocide, pro-apartheid, is not a winning strategy. And they lost handedly across the country, not just here in Michigan. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Linda, AIPAC poured so much money into defeating Dr. Abdul El-Sayed into this race. We also had yesterday morning President Trump suddenly telling Fox News that he wants to end $4 billion to Israel, and bringing up Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s name. LINDA SARSOUR : It was — you know, it’s just so ludicrous and ridiculous. And something that Dr. Abdul said during his victory speech was something that I thought was incredibly clever, where he said, “Thank you, AIPAC , for letting me beat you twice.” He beat them in the primaries. He beat them in the general election. You all know and heard that AIPAC has come out publicly saying that they will no longer endorse candidates or support candidates directly with resources. Now, people will say, “Well, of course they’re saying that now,” but they’ll find other ways to do that,” which is probably true. But the fact that they know that they are a liability, that they are toxic in politics, that nobody wants their name on them, is something — is a testament to the work that we have done in this movement to expose AIPAC’s influence in U.S. politics. And when it comes to Donald Trump, you know, Donald Trump says a lot of things. I gotta — I have to see it to believe it. But let’s just say that he is going to end the $4 billion in aid to Israel — again, a testament to the work. I don’t care how we end military aid to Israel, to be quite honest with you, as long as we end military aid to Israel. And we know that AIPAC has been lobbying against the calls to end military aid to Israel. So, either way, whether Donald Trump ends it because he doesn’t want to give someone like Abdul El-Sayed the win, I guess you can say, that’s OK with me. We just need to make sure that this apartheid, genocidal regime does not have resources, that we as Americans are not complicit in the genocide, in the violence that we’re seeing in the West Bank. I just don’t want that to be on my dime. I don’t want to be complicit in it, and neither do the American people. AMY GOODMAN : Before we go, though we’re talking to you in Michigan, where you were at the watch party last night and you also campaigned with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, we wanted to talk about Florida, as well. We have seen an extremely close race between Angie Nixon and Senator Ashley Moody. Nixon has gone down, but it was so close, and she got so little support from the Democratic Party. She was with the DSA , the Democratic Socialists of America. Can you talk about the significance of that race, where you also spent time and campaigned with Angie Nixon? LINDA SARSOUR : I had such an incredible experience multiple times over the course of the many months going to Florida, both in the primaries and in the general election. Angie Nixon is the best amongst us. She’s fearless. She’s a hustler. She was up and down the state of Florida. She was going into communities, into red communities. You name it, she was going there, and she was bringing people together. Shame on the Democratic Party. Shame on the Democratic Party, who saw a woman literally do the impossible during the primaries, had absolutely no money and was able to win by 150,000 votes against a competitor in the primary who had over $16 million. She proved it. And then she came out in the general election, and she continued to work just as hard. And the Democratic Party didn’t believe in her. If the Democratic Party would have just gave her even a tiny little fraction of what they gave to a Jon Ossoff or to a Talarico in Texas, Angie Nixon right now would be the United States senator-elect of the state of Florida. I’m so tired of the Democratic Party, who continues to say that Black voters are the foundation of the Democratic Party, and when they saw an incredibly talented, wonderful, brilliant, committed Black woman, they turned their backs on her. And so, just so you know, Amy, it’s sad, it’s outrageous, it’s frustrating, but remember this was a special election. This is only for two years. And so, we are welcoming Angie Nixon back in 2028. We got her back. And we hope that at that time the party provides her with the resources necessary for her to become the first Black woman United States senator from the great state of Florida. AMY GOODMAN : The words of Angie Nixon — now, remember, she was in a race against Ashley Moody, who was the Florida secretary of state, named to the Florida Senate seat vacated when Republican Senator Marco Rubio joined the Trump administration as U.S. secretary of state. This is Angie Nixon speaking last night. ANGIE NIXON : I am so incredibly proud of what we built together. Tonight, tonight, the results are not what we worked for. They are not what we hoped for. And I know there are a lot of people in this room and across the state that are hurting right now. But I’m an organizer, not a politician. And organizers don’t quit on the mission because one option closes. So, I want y’all to hear me when I say this: We may not have won this election, but that outcome will not stop us from getting up, from getting up tomorrow to continue the fight to deliver what everyday, hard-working Floridians need and deserve. They need a government that works for them and not the greedy corporations. I’m going to wake up tomorrow and keep fighting. AMY GOODMAN : That’s Angie Nixon in her concession speech last night in Florida, losing the race for the U.S. Senate. We want to thank Linda Sarsour for joining us from Dearborn, Michigan, but also spent time in Florida with Angie Nixon. Linda Sarsour, Palestinian American Muslim organizer, author of We Are Not Here to Be Bystanders , co-founder of MPower Action Fund.

articles.title: “The Earth Shook Last Night”: Talarico Wins Senate, Hinojosa Becomes First Latina Governor in Texas
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report , on this morning after the midterm elections. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat. ANJALI KAMAT : We turn now to Texas, where Democrats have shattered more than three decades of Republican dominance, winning races for U.S. Senate, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and even railroad commissioner. And Democrats are poised to possibly take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2003. James Talarico will be the first Democrat to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate since Lloyd Bentsen left in 1993. Talarico spoke at a victory rally Tuesday night after defeating Trump-backed MAGA Republican Ken Paxton. SEN .- ELECT JAMES TALARICO : We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love. … We were the underdogs in this race. We went up against nearly 40 years of doubt and disillusionment. We went up against more than $300 million, more than any Senate campaign in American history. We went up against all the negative ads, smear campaigns, foreign bots and AI deepfakes that money can buy. Those attacks were the final howls of a dying establishment. … We saw it in this race. We saw it in every billionaire-funded attack ad. The people at the top divide us by party, by race, by gender, by religion, by culture, so we don’t notice that they are picking our pockets, that they are defunding our schools, that they are gutting our healthcare, that they are raising taxes on all of us while they cut taxes for themselves. It is the oldest strategy in the world: divide and conquer. But tonight, we sent a crystal clear message to the people at the top: We will not be conquered. … As this movement heads to the seat of power, as we head to the United States Senate, we know what this moment requires of us. Texas, it’s time to start flipping tables. AMY GOODMAN : That was James Talarico, the Democratic senator-elect of Texas, speaking after he defeated the attorney general of Texas, Ken Paxton. When President Trump said that James Talarico was a “vagan” — that’s how he put it, talking about a vegan, saying he was a “vagan” — James Talarico’s response was “I’ve been eating Texas barbecue before Paxton was either indicted or impeached.” Meanwhile, the Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, has lost his bid for a fourth term. Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa defeated Abbott by nearly 700,000 votes. She becomes Texas’s first-ever Latina governor. GOV .- ELECT GINA HINOJOSA : We did it! Everything is bigger in Texas, including the shock of this win. We shocked the world tonight. … And now I stand before you, humbled and grateful, and in awe of the incredible grace and power of God and of Texas. I am a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, where the people embody the work ethic and values of our great state, where no one would have imagined that one day a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas. AMY GOODMAN : That’s [Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa] in her victory address last night in Austin, Texas. For more, we stay in Austin. To talk about the significance of these historic elections in Texas, we go to Mike Siegel, an Austin, Texas, City Council member, two-time Democratic nominee for Congress and the founder of Ground Game Texas, a statewide voter turnout organization. Thanks so much for joining us from Austin. We spoke to you there last night in our midterm special , which we encourage people to check out at democracynow.org and on our YouTube channel. Mike, you were at the victory party of James Talarico. If you can just talk about the significance of these two wins? MIKE SIEGEL : Well, thank you so much, Amy. It’s a wonderful morning here in Austin, Texas. And yes, the Earth shook last night. I mean, getting rid of Greg Abbott, Ken Paxton and also Dan Patrick, the lieutenant governor, just means so much to the people of Austin, the people of Texas. These three individuals caused so much harm across the state in so many different ways. And I went to Talarico’s event last night, Hinojosa’s event, other events, and everyone is just celebrating. I mean, the air was ringing with the sound of car horns last night, people yelling all across town. It’s like we won the Super Bowl or something of that nature. And people are celebrating the work of Texans, Texas Democrats, over so many electoral cycles, you know, voter registration, turnout. We’re celebrating these wonderful candidates who won office. And we’re also starting to think about what it means to hold power, the idea that Democrats will control the executive branch of government in the state of Texas. This is an event of international significance. And we need to start thinking very quickly about how we will protect public education, how we will stop data centers and the encroachment of AI on our society, you know, how how we will protect public schools, how we stop collaboration with ICE . I mean, there’s so many things people are thinking about right now. And I heard some talk last night about how we need a Project 2027 for Texas, and we need to get that together in the next couple of months, because these folks caused so much harm, and there’s so much opportunity right now to show the people of Texas a different way of government, how government can actually take care of people and make us safer, make our futures stronger. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Mike, can you talk about the significance of the Latino vote and the voter turnout, that came out for the Democratic candidates last night, and how this was a rejection of the harsh immigration enforcement policies of President Trump and, in Texas, of Governor Abbott? MIKE SIEGEL : Thank you, Anjali. Yeah, I think it’s twofold, with especially young Latino voters, you know, completely flipping the narrative in the Rio Grande Valley in South Texas. I think it was driven by both economic factors and the cruelty of ICE . I mean, the idea that the Trump administration promised lower groceries, but then enters this unnecessary and illegal war with Iran and dramatically increases the cost of living, there’s so many failed promises on the economic side of things, which really matters — right? — to working-class people. But at the same time, Governor Abbott basically used Texas as a testing ground. You know, before ICE became this new, incredibly hostile and violent and deadly organization nationwide, they were piloting programs here in Texas, whether it’s the militarization of the border through a program called Operation Lone Star, where billions of dollars that could have been spent on schools, that could have been spent on healthcare, was instead spent on, you know, border theater to show Donald Trump how good Texas is kissing up to him, and it’s also the collaboration of ICE with our state police, the Department of Public Safety. They have basically got it down to a science how state police and ICE officers can stop people for broken tail lights and other minor offenses, and then folks end up deported, even if they have legal status, even if they’re children, even if they have every reason to be here in the community. So I think the Latino community was absolutely critical, and the idea that our next governor is from Brownsville, Texas, which is, you know, among the larger cities in the United States, I think, the poorest city and a place of incredible injustice. It’s also the home base of Elon Musk and his, you know, SpaceX company. And so, the idea that we have a woman from Brownsville taking the executive branch of Texas, someone who’s going to take on Elon Musk, who’s going to hopefully end collaboration with ICE at the state level, it just means so much to the people here, and especially the Latino community. ANJALI KAMAT : And Elon Musk poured, I mean, nearly half a billion dollars to keep Republicans in power and to keep Texas red. What happened to that bet? And now, what’s at stake with all the data centers? MIKE SIEGEL : What I loved hearing from James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa on the campaign trail is how they framed this election as a battle between, you know, the billionaires and the people. And, you know, we’ve had cycles of billionaires in Texas who have taken over the political system, whether it’s these West Texas billionaires, you know, who are from the oil and gas industry, whether it’s this Pennsylvania billionaire who forced us to have, you know, vouchers in our public education system, and now Elon Musk. These folks have been absolutely distorting the political process, undermining democracy and sacrificing, you know, working people, ordinary Texans, for their own profits. And so, the idea that this grassroots movement across the state, you know, led by our standard-bearers on the Democratic Party ticket, that we were able to defeat Elon, defeat these billionaire interests, despite being outspent, it means so much. At the same time, we can’t celebrate too much. Obviously, last night was amazing. And, oh man, the social media feeds right now of people just celebrating all the blood, sweat and tears is just so healthy. It’s a wonderful thing right now that all of us are experiencing right now. But we have to take this so seriously that, really, Democrats in Texas have four years to deliver — right? — to show a different way of politics, a different way of government, whether that’s restoring public education, whether that’s expanding healthcare. You know, Abbott refused Medicaid expansion. We have the highest maternal mortality rate in the country, especially among Black women. On environmental issues, on surveillance, the idea that Abbott was supporting the proliferation of Flock cameras and, yes, you know, giving all these tax benefits to AI and data center companies to buy up land, to jack up land values, to raise our electric and water rates — all of these issues are the reasons why we won. I mean, there were so many issues that were in our favor, and our leading candidates — AMY GOODMAN : We — MIKE SIEGEL : — took the right side. Sorry, and I’ll go back to y’all. But I just think — I think we have a lot of work to do to keep the momentum, of course. AMY GOODMAN : And we want to thank you, Mike Siegel, for being with us. One of the most touching scenes yesterday was in Houston. In Houston, in July, the 52-year-old Mexican national, longtime U.S. resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was shot and killed by an ICE agent. Yesterday, his son Ronaldo voted, and then he took his “I just voted” sticker and put it at the memorial for his father. And then, one Texan after another, after they came out of the voting booth, put their sticker there, too, remembering the man who was killed by ICE in Houston, Texas, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Mike Siegel, we want to thank you so much for being with us, Austin, Texas, City Council member, two-time Democratic nominee for Congress, founder of Ground Game Texas, a statewide voter turnout organization. When we come back, we continue to look at historic wins. We go to Georgia to speak with Emory professor Carol Anderson about the victory of the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Nora Brown and Stephanie Coleman.

articles.title: Protest near Kyiv exposes detention of AWOL soldiers
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: On Monday, November 2, protesters gathered in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka in the Kyiv region, outside a building that was used as a detention site holding soldiers absent without leave and recruits. Facing army and police forces, alongside non-uniformed attackers, protesters were able to bring out the men held inside. Many of the men who left the building displayed signs of physical violence. Four men – confirmed to be soldiers absent without leave – were hospitalized, while videos from the ground testimonies showed others as battered and bruised. The detention site was associated with the Azov Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine. The formation described using the premises as a “temporary deployment” location for mobilized soldiers and men detained after going AWOL. Ukraine’s Azov formations have been long-associated to fascist ideology. Their supporters are believed to be among the non-uniformed attackers on Monday, based on the nationalist slogans chanted at the protest site. Read more: ‘Ukraine is no longer a sovereign country,’ says sociologist Volodymyr Ishchenko “One important development in last night’s events around the illegal Azov prison for deserters and draft dodgers, which also served to extort ransoms and provoked a massive riot on Kyiv’s outskirts, is the use of Azov paramilitaries to suppress the protesters,” wrote Ukrainian sociologist Volodymyr Ishchenko , adding that researchers including Oleksiy Kuzmenko had predicted this outcome. “This adds a new, characteristically fascist nuance to the events.” “Otherwise, the events manifest the same escalating dynamics of post-Soviet disintegration in Ukraine’s state and society, to which the maidan deficient revolutions greatly contributed and which the war did not resolve but only escalated,” Ishchenko added. Authorities turn against protesters After the detention site was discovered, Ukrainian officials alleged the protests were orchestrated from abroad – supposedly by Russia – and turned to punitive measures against participants. At least one person, a medic who appears in video from the scene, has reportedly been detained. National security officials announced roughly 100 people had been identified and that repercussions were being considered as well. Ukrainian authorities denied the house had been used for physical abuse. However, officials’ statements confirmed the site had been used to hold soldiers, “including those who had returned after leaving their military units without authorization.” According to Euronews , state investigators also launched inquiries into “possible abuse of authority by military officials” and “the conditions in which servicemen were accommodated.” On the night of the protest, Kyrylo Budanov , the head of Volodymyr Zelensky’s office, said there are “many more” buildings of this kind across the country. Forced street mobilizations in Ukraine persist Events in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka overlap with a continuous wave of civilian opposition to forced street mobilization in Ukraine, known as busification, amid record-low numbers of volunteer recruits. In the hours after the protest near Kyiv, more video reports circulated on social media documenting physical abuse and what could be described as state-sanctioned kidnapping of men into the armed forces. In an interview with BreakThrough News earlier this year, Ishchenko described the extent and intensity of the practice, emphasizing that people were resisting it with growing intensity. “This resistance is growing and becoming more frequent, perhaps showing qualitative advances too,” he said in July. “Until now, most resistance was spontaneous, passersby or relatives trying to help a guy escape from minibuses. There was no organization or evidence of coordination between different initiatives. But recently, it has taken on a more massive scale, like riots.”

articles.title: UN mission on Western Sahara lapses after vote deadlock in security council
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The United Nations Security Council failed to reach an agreement on the future of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) following a contentious meeting on October 30, leaving the mission without a renewed mandate for the first time since its establishment in 1991. The meeting saw Russia veto a United States-sponsored draft resolution that had received 11 votes in favor, one against, and three abstentions. The proposed resolution sought to renew the mission’s mandate for another year while making significant changes to its name, structure and political framework, including making Morocco’s autonomy proposal the basis for negotiations over the territory. This session was followed closely precisely for this reason, as the proposal would have had far-reaching consequences for the people of Sahrawi in their quest for self determination. A competing Russian-sponsored draft, which proposed a straightforward one-year extension of MINURSO’s existing mandate without changing its name or structure, also failed to secure adoption. It received three votes in favor, one against, and 11 abstentions, falling short of the nine votes required for adoption. The failure of both proposals means that the mission’s mandate expired at midnight on October 31, bringing its 35-year presence in Western Sahara to an end and raising questions about the future of the UN’s role in the territory. MINURSO was established through Security Council Resolution 690 (1991), following the UN-Organization of African Unity settlement plan accepted by Morocco and the Polisario Front in 1988. Its original mandate included preparing a referendum through which the Sahrawi people would choose between independence and integration with Morocco. However, the referendum has never been held. Morocco celebrates the end of MINURSO’s mandate Morocco welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate, describing the development as a significant step towards ending the Western Sahara question at the United Nations. In a statement issued on October 30 , the Moroccan Royal Office said the mission’s non-renewal meant its personnel, vehicles, equipment, and other presence in what Morocco refers to as its southern provinces were expected to leave in the coming days. “A 35-year chapter has now come to a close,” the statement said. Morocco further argued that the mission had outlived its original purpose and called for an end to the Security Council’s periodic consideration of the Western Sahara question, including its meetings, reports by the UN Secretary-General and briefings by his Personal Envoy. Polisario Front rejects the proposed changes The Polisario Front, which represents the Sahrawi independence movement, welcomed Russia’s opposition to the US-sponsored resolution, arguing that its adoption would have undermined the foundations of the UN-led peace process. In a communiqué issued on October 31, the movement said the deadlock resulted primarily from the US proposal, which it argued reflected the positions of Washington and Morocco while departing from the mutually-accepted framework under which MINURSO was established. The movement expressed appreciation for Russia’s veto and acknowledged the abstentions of China, Pakistan and Somalia. It also recognized the position of Algeria and other countries that have supported the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination. The Frente POLISARIO maintained that any attempt to unilaterally alter the mission’s mandate to accommodate Morocco’s position was unacceptable. It further recalled that it had submitted an expanded proposal to the UN secretary-general on October 20, 2025, as part of its stated commitment to finding a negotiated settlement. The movement reaffirmed its willingness to cooperate with the UN secretary-general and Security Council towards what it described as a just, lasting, and definitive solution to the decolonization of Western Sahara. Sahrawi organizations warn against abandoning international responsibility The failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate has also raised concerns among Sahrawi human rights organizations about the future of international monitoring and protection in the territory. The Sahrawi Collective of Human Rights Defenders in Western Sahara (CODESA) warned that the Security Council’s failure to reach an agreement should not become an opportunity for the international community to retreat from its responsibilities towards Western Sahara. In its October 31 statement , CODESA stressed that the territory remains an unresolved decolonization question and that the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination must be respected. The organization argued that the difficulties MINURSO has faced in implementing its original mandate should not be used to justify abandoning the mission. Instead, it calls for renewed efforts to enable the mission to carry out its responsibilities, particularly monitoring the ceasefire and reporting developments on the ground. CODESA also called for the establishment of an independent UN mechanism to monitor and report on the human rights situation in Western Sahara, citing the need to protect civilians and human rights defenders. Urging the Security Council to resume consultations, preserve MINURSO’s original mandate and avoid imposing a political settlement without the free consent of the Sahrawi people. UN maintains commitment to self-determination Following the expiry of the mission’s mandate, UN Secretary-General António Guterres reiterated that the end of MINURSO did not extinguish the Sahrawi people’s right to determine their political future. In a statement delivered through his spokesperson on November 1, Guterres said the departure of MINURSO “does not abrogate” the people’s “inalienable right to self-determination.” He further called on all parties to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara. The secretary-general maintained that the United Nations remained committed to supporting a just, lasting, and mutually-acceptable political solution that provides for the self-determination of the Sahrawi people. Although MINURSO’s operations are now winding down, the UN has indicated that its wider diplomatic efforts towards a peaceful resolution will continue. The failure of the Security Council to renew MINURSO’s mandate is a significant development in the long-running Western Sahara dispute. However, it does not resolve the underlying disagreement over the territory’s political status of the Sahrawian people.

articles.title: Thousands join protests in New Delhi denouncing electoral manipulation
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Hundreds of thousands took to India’s capital, New Delhi, on Sunday, November 1, to demand the sacking of the country’s Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) over allegations of manipulation and rigging various elections in India. The protesters marched in smaller groups from different corners of the city in the early morning finally converging at the central Ramlila Maidan under the call to “save democracy” made by the main block of opposition parties called the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance, or INDIA. The protesters carried banners and posters displaying their demands and waving flags of their respective political affiliations, such as the Indian National Congress (INC), left parties, and several other regional political and civil society groups. They shouted slogans against the CEC, calling him a “thief,” and the ultra-right-wing government led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, calling him “illegal.” The protesters alleged that the Modi government misused the country’s electoral body to deprive millions of people of their right to vote in order to manage electoral victories. Calling it the “murder of democracy” the protesters have been demanding the end of the so-called SIR process, the re-inclusion of all the names removed from the country’s electoral rolls, and the sacking of Gyanesh Kumar, the CEC. SIR or the Special Intensive Revision of the electoral rolls, launched last year, has led to the removal of over 130 million voters, around 14% of all electorates registered in the country. The opposition claims the exclusion was targeted at voters who generally do not vote for the ruling Hindu supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), namely the voters from religious minority communities and socially and economically-deprived sections of society. Sunday’s protests marked yet another surge in the months-long nationwide protests which began early in October. The initial protests, mostly led by youth under the banner of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) intensified after the publication of reports about the CEC violating basic procedures to implement arbitrary decisions about the SIR. The anti-government protests have faced strong state repression including the arrest of some of its leaders, blocking of all major entries to central Delhi, banning protests at designated sites, and mass detentions. Even on Sunday, several protesters from far away places complained that the government tried to prevent them from reaching Delhi. The government and pro-government media tried to blame the protesters for creating chaos in the country and harming businesses in Delhi. Protesters have dismissed the allegations, calling them “fear mongering” tactics typical of BJP attempts to demonize the opposition. Accountability for stealing votes Several leaders of the opposition parties and members of the civil society groups addressed the protesters, pointing out the major demands and warning of more protests if the government fails to respond to them. Reiterating his allegations against the CEC of “treason” against the country by “stealing the votes,” Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main centrist opposition party, the INC, demanded accountability. He promised that no matter how much time it takes Gyanesh Kumar will pay for his crimes against Indian democracy. Gandhi termed the movement against Gyanesh Kumar a “second freedom struggle” of India. A day earlier, the opposition had staged a “public impeachment” of Gyanesh Kumar. He was pronounced guilty of stealing the votes and failing to discharge his duties impartially. The CEC is a constitutional post and cannot be removed without an “impeachment motion” adopted by the parliament. During Sunday’s rally, several other speakers repeated the point and spoke about the violence and repression unleashed on the protesters last month. They assured the people that all those responsible for such criminal activities will face the rule of law. Speaking to the protesters, M A Baby, general secretary of the CPI (M) called the action of electoral fraud a “fascist tactic.” He alleged that the government and particularly Prime Minister Modi have been lying to people and misleading them on various issues and for a democracy it is must that they are held accountable for their crimes against the people. Several leaders including Rahul Gandhi also questioned the 2024 national elections and other state legislative elections calling they were “stolen” by the ruling BJP. They claimed that the Prime Minister of the country was “illegal” and it was necessary to dissolve the current parliament and fresh elections were held. Despite losing its majority in the 2024 national elections, the BJP came back to power with the support of allies for a third consecutive term. The elections were marred with allegations of manipulation and voter suppression. The gathering in Ramlila Maidan ended with warning of more protests in the coming days and intensification of the movement if the government fails to acknowledge its failings and sacks Gyanesh Kumar.

articles.title: Israeli forces withdraw from Hebron following 11-day large-scale operation
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: The Israeli forces withdrew from the West Bank southern city of Hebron on Monday, November 2, after carrying out an extensive military operation that saw the displacement of hundreds of families and massive destruction of residential buildings over the span of 11 days. The operation, which included a full lockdown of the West Bank and was considered by many as a collective punishment of the entire Palestinian population in the occupied territory, was launched on October 23, after two Israeli soldiers were shot dead by two Palestinian men near a military checkpoint in the Farsh al-Hawa area. According to Hebron Municipality, 15 homes and facilities were demolished in the assault, while 327 shops were closed, with direct daily economic losses estimated at roughly $3.8 million. The municipality had earlier reported that at least 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families were displaced as a result of the offensive. Meanwhile, the governor of Hebron, Khaled Doudin, stated that about 600 homes in the areas that were subjected to raids and searches by the Israeli military were damaged. The operation ended, yet arrest campaigns and restriction on movement continue in the city Although the large-scale operation in Hebron apparently ended, a sweeping arrest campaign was carried out on Tuesday, November 3, during which 21 Palestinians were detained by the Israeli army in Dura, southwest of the city. On the same day, the army forced an extended family of 15 individuals to evacuate their home in the village of Al-Burj, southwest of Hebron, turning it into a military barrack. Several checkpoints were also set up at the entrances of the city and different towns, villages and refugee camps within the governorate, while movement was further restricted with iron gates, concrete blocks, and earthen barriers being installed along main and side roads. On the day of their withdrawal from the city, the Israeli forces stormed the campus of Kadoorie University, in the Al-Aroub area north of Hebron. One young man was briefly detained during the raid, but he was released before the troops departed the academic facility.

articles.title: China calls on US to end blockade on Cuba and respect its sovereignty
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: A day after joining the overwhelming majority of countries in the UN General Assembly to vote on a resolution demanding the lifting of the US blockade and sanctions on Cuba, China called on the US to immediately stop its threats of force against the country. “The illegal economic embargo and unilateral economic sanctions imposed by the US against Cuba have lasted for 64 years inflicting untold suffering on Cuban people,” Guo Jiakun, official spokesperson of China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said during a regular press conference on Thursday, October 29. Claiming that “the overwhelming majority of countries in the world are outraged by the US’s serious violation of the purposes and principles of the UN Charter,” China reiterated the “international community’s longstanding call for the US to immediately stop infringing on the Cuban people’s right to survive and thrive.” On Wednesday, 130 countries voted in favor of a resolution in the UN General Assembly demanding the end of decades of unilateral US sanctions and blockade on Cuba. This was the 34th consecutive time since 1992 that the UNGA had adopted the resolution holding the US responsible for violating Cuba’s right to self-determination and other international laws. Though the US embargo and unilateral sanctions against Cuba are decades old, they have intensified since Donald Trump came to power for the second term last year. The economic blockade has particularly created massive shortages of essential goods and services such as fuel, electricity, food, and medicine, affecting millions on the island nation. The embargo has caused disruptions in medical services and impacted basic sectors of the Cuban economy, rendering thousands of people jobless, with the UN warning of “humanitarian collapse” if it continues. Cuba has claimed that US sanctions and embargoes cause over eight billion in losses to the country’s economy every year. Some countries, including China, have tried to assist Cuba by providing humanitarian food and energy supplies. Stop threats of use of force Calling Cuba’s revolutionary government “authoritarian” and labeling the country as a “sponsor of terrorism,” successive US administrations have tried to stage “regime change” in the country through covert and overt means, completely disregarding the Cuban people’s right to self-determination and their own obligations under international law. The Trump administration, after declaring Cuba “an unusual and extraordinary threat” last year, tightened the blockade and has even threatened to launch military operations against the country. It has demanded the Cuban government make policy changes based on Washington’s wishes. During the ongoing midterm campaign, Trump has reportedly claimed that the war against Cuba was imminent and can begin the moment the US armed forces were free from the war against Iran. Cuba has rejected US allegations and refused to surrender its sovereignty despite threats of war. Apart from providing humanitarian aid, China has also warned against such threats of military interventions raising the issue on various international forums, including the UN. Asking the Trump administration to “heed the call for justice from the international community,” Guo Jiakun reiterated on Thursday the Chinese demand that “the US stop all forms of coercion and pressure on Cuba, including through the threat of force.” Guo also reiterated that “China will continue firmly supporting Cuba’s just effort for safeguarding national sovereignty and dignity, and opposing external interference and embargo.” The reiteration of Chinese support follows its earlier pronouncement of support to Cuba’s revolutionary government “no matter how the international landscape evolves.” China, while observing 66 years of diplomatic relations with Cuba last month, had claimed that the “socialist development path” suited Cuba’s national conditions and helped in safeguarding its national sovereignty and opposing external interference.” Recognizing how Cuba was the first Latin American country to recognize the People’s Republic of China in 1960, Guo Jiakun claimed that, in recent years, the two countries have made “sustained and steady progress” in building a “community with a shared future.”
